title: The Hidden Curriculum for Adults: Why School Norms Shape Teachers More Than Policies
author: Dr Haili Hughes
summary: School culture and informal norms exert more influence on teacher behavior than formal policies or leadership directives. Drawing on cognitive science — particularly Kahneman’s System 1 thinking and McCrea’s model of motivation as unconscious investment — Hughes argues that teachers scan their environments for social cues before consciously deliberating, making the hidden curriculum of the staffroom as powerful as any professional development programme. Social Identity Theory explains why this matters: teachers constantly seek signals about what “people like us do around here,” making peer norms the dominant force in shaping professional behavior. Hughes contrasts two school cultures — one where martyrdom and cynicism are the unspoken norm, and one where curiosity and sustainability prevail — and notes that neither emerges from deliberate policy but from accumulated habit. Wellbeing, she argues, is not an individual trait but a collective achievement: when prevailing norms stigmatize asking for help or reward exhaustion as virtue, no amount of wellbeing programming will change outcomes. The practical implication for leaders is to shape the environment rather than persuade through argument — making desirable behaviors visible, allowing respected colleagues to leave at sensible hours without apology, and cultivating psychological safety. Like pupils, teachers learn what professionalism means through daily interaction with colleagues; the hidden curriculum for adults is every bit as influential as the formal one. The final question is not whether norms exist — they always do — but whether they are being shaped deliberately or merely inherited from the loudest voices in the room.
points: School norms shape teacher behavior more powerfully than formal policies because most human decision-making is unconscious and relies on social heuristics — teachers observe what the people around them do and adjust automatically, often before conscious reflection begins.

Kahneman’s System 1 thinking and McCrea’s motivation model explain why persuasion-based leadership so often fails: the brain defaults to fast, social shortcuts, meaning the staffroom environment teaches professional identity more effectively than any policy document or training day.

Social Identity Theory (Tajfel and Turner) shows that teachers constantly ask “what do people like me do around here?” — making peer culture the dominant force shaping behavior, for better or worse, regardless of what leaders intend.

Wellbeing is a collective, norm-driven achievement rather than an individual characteristic: when prevailing norms stigmatize help-seeking, reward presenteeism, or make perfectionism the measure of professionalism, explicit wellbeing initiatives cannot address the root cause.

Leaders who want to change culture must engineer the environment — making desirable behaviors visibly normal through role modelling and structural affordances — rather than relying on rationale and evidence presentations that engage the slow, deliberate System 2 at the expense of the faster System 1 that actually drives most behavior.
quotes: Schools spend enormous amounts of time writing policies that describe how people should behave. Yet, as Doug Lemov argues, norms almost always prove more influential than rules because they shape behaviour beneath conscious awareness. They are “largely invisible and unconscious,” yet often override formal policies because they determine what people come to regard as normal.

In the first, the dominant conversations revolve around workload, difficult pupils and the latest educational initiative that “will all be forgotten by Christmas.” Professional reading is treated with affectionate suspicion. Teachers who leave before five o’clock are jokingly referred to as “part-timers”, while martyrdom enjoys an oddly elevated social status.

If the prevailing norm suggests that asking for help signals weakness, teachers will quietly struggle alone. If staying until seven o’clock becomes synonymous with commitment, workload will expand to fill the available time. If perfectionism becomes the unofficial measure of professionalism, exhaustion slowly acquires the status of virtue.

Rather than repeatedly telling teachers that collaboration matters, make collaboration visible. Rather than encouraging wellbeing, allow respected colleagues to leave at sensible times without apology. Rather than celebrating resilience, celebrate sustainability.

Perhaps that is the most important lesson of all. Every school is constantly teaching its staff what professionalism looks like, whether intentionally or accidentally. The question is not whether norms exist - they always do. The question is whether we are shaping them deliberately or merely inheriting them from the loudest voices in the room.
